parole.significato: to indicate something through gesture, such as waving one’s hand, nodding or moving one’s eyes
parole.testo: From a- + Early Medieval Latin cinnāre (“blink”).

parole.significato: to cover with a coat, jacket or a blanket; to wrap up
parole.testo: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin gasalia (“housemate, companion”), from Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐍃𐌰𐌻𐌹 (*gasali, “company”), from Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐍃𐌰𐌻𐌾𐌰 (*gasalja, “companion”), from Proto-Germanic *gasaljô (“housemate, companion”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese alumẽar, from Early Medieval Latin allūmināre. Compare Galician alumear, Spanish alumbrar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese amarelo (“yellow”), from Early Medieval Latin amārellus (“yellowish, pale”). Compare Galician amarelo, Fala amarelu, Mirandese amarielho, Spanish amarillo.

parole.significato: to walk (to move on one’s feet)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese andar, from Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: to repent (to feel bad about one’s past misdeeds)
parole.testo: From a- + Old Galician-Portuguese repender, repeender, from Early Medieval Latin repoenitēre, from Latin paenitēre. Suffixation perhaps to avoid confusion with the unrelated Portuguese pender (“hang”). Compare Galician arrepentir, Spanish arrepentirse.

parole.significato: to arrive (at a port); to bear away (from the wind)
parole.testo: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre. By surface analysis, a- + riba + -ar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese biscoito, from Early Medieval Latin biscoctus (literally “twice-baked”). Compare Galician biscoito, Spanish bizcocho. Doublet of biscuit.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese branco, from Early Medieval Latin blancus, borrowed from Frankish *blank. Cognate with Galician branco, Spanish blanco. Doublet of Blanco and Bianca.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese calça, from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caminho, from Late Latin cammīnus (“way”), from Gaulish. Compare Galician camiño.

Probably from Old Galician-Portuguese capelo, from Early Medieval Latin cappellus (“hat”), diminutive from Late Latin cappa, or less likely through Italian cappello (although this probably applies in the sense of a cardinal's red hat). Doublet of chapéu, which came through French.

parole.significato: path, trail (particularly one which had to be opened)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese carreira, from Early Medieval Latin via carrāria, from Latin carrus, from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós, from *ḱers- (“to run”).. Compare Galician carreira and Spanish carrera. Cognate with also English career. By surface analysis, carro + -

parole.significato: each of the side boards of an ox cart containing the holes for the stanchions
parole.testo: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin clēta.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese choca, from Early Medieval Latin clocca (“bell”), from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (“bell”). Compare English clock and French cloche (“bell”) and Irish clog (“bell, clock”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese desejo, from Early Medieval Latin dēsideus (“desire”), from Latin dēsidia (“sloth, debauchery”). Compare Galician desexo, Asturian deséu, Spanish deseo, Aragonese deseyo, Sicilian disiju.
From Old Galician-Portuguese desfazer, from Early Medieval Latin desfacere. Synchronically des- + fazer.
From Early Medieval Latin impeiōrāre, from Latin peiōrem (“worse”). By surface analysis, em- + pior + -ar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese enganar, from Early Medieval Latin ingannāre (“to trick, to deceive”) (attested in a gloss), from Latin gannīre. Compare Spanish engañar, Italian ingannare.
Ultimately from Early Medieval Latin foresta. Influenced by flor (“flower”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese geada, from Early Medieval Latin gelāta, derived from Latin gelāre (“freeze”). By surface analysis, gear (“to frost”) + -ada. Doublet of gelada and geleia. Compare Galician xeada, Spanish helada, Catalan gelada, French gelée and Italian gelata.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese guardar, from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese guerra, from Early Medieval Latin werra, borrowed from Frankish *werʀu, from Proto-West Germanic *werʀan + *-u.. Related to the word varrer.

parole.significato: to lead; to guide; to direct
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese guiar, from Early Medieval Latin guidāre, possibly from Gothic *𐍅𐌹𐌳𐌰𐌽 (*widan, “to join”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese madrỹa, from Early Medieval Latin mātrīna, from Latin mater (“mother”). Compare Galician madriña.

parole.significato: handle (part of an object which is held in the hand)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mango, from Early Medieval Latin manicus, from Latin manus (“hand”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese mealla, from Early Medieval Latin medālia (“middle; half a denarius”), ultimately from Latin medius. Doublet of medalha, which was borrowed through Italian.

parole.significato: bailiff (legal officer with some degree of authority)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese meyrĩo, from Early Medieval Latin maiōrīnus. Cognate with Spanish merino.

From Old Galician-Portuguese mezclar, mezcrar, mizclar, mizcrar, from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin miscēre (“mix”). Compare Spanish mezclar, Catalan mesclar, French mêler, Italian mischiare, mescolare.
From Old Galician-Portuguese montanna, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin officāre, alteration of Latin offōcāre. Doublet of afogar.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin auctoricāre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese padrinho, from Early Medieval Latin patrīnus (“godfather”), from Latin pater (“father”), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr (“father”). Compare Galician padriño.
Borrowed from Gallo-Romance (cf. Catalan and Occitan parlar, French parler), from Early Medieval Latin parabolāre.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin pollicipēs, from pollex (“thumb”) + pēs (“foot”).

parole.significato: flat seed (such as those of a pumpkin, melon, or pear)
parole.testo: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin pipita. Doublet of pituíta.

parole.significato: hamlet (small village or a group of houses)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese póvoa (“land to be peopled”), from Early Medieval Latin popula, a derivative of populus. Cognate Galician Poboa, Spanish Puebla and Pobla.

parole.significato: registration (act of signing up or registering for something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese registro, registo, from Early Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regerere (“to record, to carry back”), from re- + gerere (“to carry, bear”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese ribeira, from Early Medieval Latin rīpāria.

parole.significato: rein (strap or rope used to control an animal)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese redẽa, from Early Medieval Latin retina, ultimately from Latin retinere (“hold back, restrain”). Compare Galician rédea, renda and Spanish rienda.
From Old Galician-Portuguese sãadyo, from Early Medieval Latin sānātīvus, from Latin sānātus, from sānō, from sānus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese sendeiro, from Early Medieval Latin sēmitārius, derived from Latin sēmita. Compare Galician sendeiro, Spanish sendero.

parole.significato: to be (to have the given quality), especially a quality that is intrinsic or not expected to change, contrasting with e…
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ser, from Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse. The forms sou (“I am”) and sois pl (“you are”) derive from a Vulgar Latin *sonō and *sutis. Along the way, the verb absorbed Old Galician-Portuguese seer < Latin sedēre (“sit”). The latter supplied the present subju
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese setembro, setenbro, from Early Medieval Latin Septembrius, from Latin September.
From Old Galician-Portuguese soomente~soamente, from Early Medieval Latin sōlā mente. By surface analysis, só + -mente.

From a Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin tenda, from Vulgar Latin *tendita, substantivized feminine of *tenditus, as a variant form of tentus, perfect passive participle of Latin tendō. Compare Italian tenda, Spanish tienda, French tente.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese trago, from Early Medieval Latin tragō.

parole.significato: to use; to utilise; to employ; to make use of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese usar, from Early Medieval Latin ūsāre.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin vaccārius. By surface analysis, vaca + -eiro. Compare Spanish vaquero. The sense of "cowboy" is a semantic loan from English cowboy.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin verēda (“path, main road”), from Latin verēdus (“light breed of horse”), borrowed from Gaulish *werēdos, from Proto-Celtic *uɸoreidos, from *uɸo- + *reidos.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vẽeira, from Early Medieval Latin veneria, from Latin Venus. Doublet of venera. Cognate with Galician vieira and Spanish venera.
From Old Galician-Portuguese renda, probably from Old Catalan or Old Occitan renda, either way from Early Medieval Latin rendita. Compare Galician renda, Spanish renta.
